sections.heading: Receiving your greatest gift
sections.text: Father, every good thing comes from you. What could I ever give back to you for the gift above every gift—your own beloved Son? He was not made; he is eternally your Son. Yet you gave him for me: my Redeemer, my representative, my guarantor, my substitute. I cannot get my mind around the depth of his humility or the endless reach of his love.
theological_themes: God is the source of every good gift.
The Son is eternally divine, not a created being.
Christ is given by the Father as Redeemer, representative, surety, and substitute for sinners.
The incarnation displays humility and immeasurable love.

scripture_references.connection: James teaches that every good and perfect gift comes from God, which grounds the prayer’s opening confession that the Son himself is the supreme gift from the Father.
This passage presents the Father giving his only Son out of love so that sinners may have eternal life through him, directly supporting the prayer’s gratitude for Christ as God’s greatest gift.
Paul describes the Son as preeminent over creation and the one through whom reconciliation is made, supporting both Christ’s divine status and his saving work.

sections.heading: Marveling at the Son who came down for me
sections.text: This is wonder beyond anything I can explain: he came down into my low place so he could lift me up. He was born as one of us so that I could be made like him. When I could not climb up to you, he came near to me in grace and carried me toward himself.
theological_themes: The incarnation is God’s gracious descent to sinners who cannot reach him by their own strength.
Christ became truly human to bring believers into conformity with himself.
Salvation begins with God’s initiative, not human ascent.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes the eternal Son humbling himself by taking human form and going to the cross, which gives biblical shape to the prayer’s wonder that Christ came low to lift sinners up.
This passage frames Christ’s self-giving in terms of his becoming poor so that his people might become rich, closely matching the prayer’s movement from Christ’s descent to the believer’s elevation.
Paul says God’s saving purpose is to conform believers to the image of his Son, supporting the prayer’s claim that Christ became like us so that we might become like him.

sections.heading: Trusting the wisdom and power of the incarnation
sections.text: Here I see your power and wisdom. You bridged what I never could: the holy God and fallen humanity, the uncreated Son and created flesh, joined forever in one person. I was ruined, and I did not even have the will to come back to you or the wisdom to rescue myself. So he came as God with us—able to save completely.
theological_themes: In Christ, true deity and true humanity are united in one person.
Human beings are helpless to save themselves apart from God’s grace.
The incarnation is the wise and powerful way God brings salvation.

scripture_references.connection: John states that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, grounding the prayer’s confession that the uncreated Son truly took on created humanity.
Paul identifies Christ Jesus as the one mediator between God and humanity, which supports the prayer’s focus on the incarnate Son bridging the divide sinners could not cross.
Hebrews teaches that Christ is able to save completely those who come to God through him, echoing the prayer’s confidence that God-incarnate saves to the uttermost.

sections.heading: Resting in what Jesus did in my place
sections.text: Lord Jesus, you came as a real man to die the death I deserved. You shed blood that truly answers for my sin. You lived the perfect obedience I never lived, and you give me a righteousness I could never produce. My hope is not in my effort, my regret, or my religious performance. My hope is in you.
theological_themes: Christ died as a substitute for sinners.
Christ’s blood satisfies the demands of justice and brings forgiveness.
Christ’s perfect righteousness is counted to believers by faith.
Salvation rests on Christ’s finished work, not human merit.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that Christ, though sinless, was made sin for us so that we might become righteous in him, directly supporting the prayer’s language of substitution and received righteousness.
Peter presents Christ as bearing our sins in his body on the tree, which grounds the prayer’s confession that Jesus died the death sinners deserved.
This passage explains that sinners are justified by God’s grace through Christ’s redemptive work and blood, supporting the prayer’s trust in Christ’s atoning death rather than personal merit.

sections.heading: Standing at the manger in faith and joy
sections.text: Father, take me in my heart to the shepherds keeping watch that night. Open my mind to the good news of great joy. Let me hear it again—not as a familiar story only, but as news for me. Help me believe it, rejoice in it, praise you for it, and worship. Let my conscience be quieted by your peace, and let me lift my eyes to you as my reconciled Father.
theological_themes: The birth of Christ is good news of great joy for sinners.
Faith responds to the gospel with joy, praise, and worship.
Because of Christ, the conscience can rest and the believer can approach God as reconciled Father.

scripture_references.connection: Luke records the angelic announcement to the shepherds and their response of worship, making this the direct biblical background for the prayer’s request to hear, believe, rejoice, and adore.
Paul says justification by faith brings peace with God through Jesus Christ, supporting the prayer’s longing for a quieted conscience before a reconciled Father.
Hebrews connects Christ’s priestly work with confident access to God and a cleansed conscience, illuminating the prayer’s movement from beholding Christ to resting before the Father.

sections.heading: Holding Christ as mine
sections.text: Put me low beside the animals at the manger, content simply to look at the face of my Redeemer and know that in him I am set free from sin. Let me be like Simeon, receiving Christ with both arms of faith, holding him close, and rejoicing that he is mine and I am his. In him, Father, you have given me so much that even heaven itself has nothing greater to add.
theological_themes: Faith personally receives and embraces Christ.
In Christ, the believer belongs to him and is delivered from sin.
Christ himself is the fullness of God’s gift; there is no greater treasure than him.

scripture_references.connection: Simeon receives the infant Christ and praises God for seeing his salvation, which directly supports the prayer’s desire to embrace Christ with faith and joy.
John describes receiving Christ and believing in his name as the way people are given the right to become children of God, supporting the prayer’s personal appropriation of Christ.
Paul says believers are in Christ Jesus, who has become their wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption, reinforcing the prayer’s conclusion that all saving riches are found in him.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original strongly assumes Nicene Christology, especially that the Son is begotten, not created. I preserved this because it is central to the prayer’s meaning, though the exact phrase is creedal rather than a direct biblical quotation.

The prayer’s language of Christ as ‘proxy, surety, substitute’ reflects a Reformed account of atonement, including substitution and imputed righteousness. These themes are doctrinally contested among some Christian traditions but are clearly intended in the source.

The original manger scene includes animals named in traditional nativity imagination. The canonical Gospels mention a manger but do not explicitly list those animals. I kept the image in a restrained way as a devotional scene rather than a claim about what Scripture explicitly records.
significant_interpretive_choices: I rendered ‘when I cannot rise to him he draws near on wings of grace’ as God’s gracious initiative toward someone unable to climb up to him, preserving the original emphasis on grace without keeping the older image.

I interpreted ‘he came below to raise me above’ and ‘was born like me that I might become like him’ as the incarnation leading to salvation and conformity to Christ, not as deification in a technical sense.
I treated ‘satisfying blood’ as Christ’s atoning death satisfying divine justice, because the surrounding phrases about substitute, death, and righteousness point in that direction.
I kept the final line’s force by saying heaven has nothing greater to add, meaning Christ himself is the supreme gift, not that the believer has no future hope of heaven.
